analysis.one_liner: Overhauls campaign finance by capping House spending, banning party soft money, and tightening PAC and disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: A campaign finance bill with 46 bipartisan cosponsors never received a hearing or a vote in any House committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal campaign finance law. House candidates who agreed to a $600,000 spending cap would get cheap TV and radio time and discounted postage, while national parties and federal candidates would be barred from raising unregulated "soft money." It also tightened PAC limits, banned leadership PACs, required faster disclosure of big independent ad campaigns, barred contributions from people who cannot legally vote, and stopped officeholders from spending campaign money on personal expenses or election-year mass mailings.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would see the flow of large unregulated donations to the parties cut off and get faster disclosure of who is paying for campaign ads. Small donors and financially average candidates would benefit from the $600,000 spending cap plus broadcast and postage discounts, which would make running against a wealthy self-funder more feasible. Candidates who comply would get half-price ad time during the final 30 and 60 days before an election.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, small donors, and non-wealthy candidates

how_it_helps.text: Bans the national party committees and federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting or spending 'soft money' — the unlimited, unregulated donations that had become the parties' main funding channel — and requires state party spending that affects federal elections to come from regulated funds.

Lets House candidates who voluntarily accept a $600,000 spending cap (plus a 60%-in-state small-donor requirement and a 10% cap on personal-fund use) claim half-price broadcast time in the closing 30/60 days and reduced postage rates, lowering the cost of running for office for people without personal wealth or big-donor networks.

Cuts PAC leverage over House candidates by capping total PAC money at 25% of the spending limit, bans leadership PACs that members used to stockpile and redistribute influence, and caps large individual contributions at 25% of the spending limit per candidate.

Requires disclosure within 24-48 hours of large independent ad campaigns and coordinated spending, treats lobbyist-arranged bundled contributions as coming from the lobbyist, extends the foreign-contribution ban to anyone not qualified to register to vote, and adds random audits, faster FEC procedures, larger penalties, and mandatory electronic filing.

Restricts officeholders' personal use of campaign funds (mortgages, vacations, club dues and the like) and bans election-year franked mass mailings, which incumbents had used as free taxpayer-funded self-promotion.

analysis.who_pays: National and state party committees would lose the soft money pipeline (partly offset by a raised individual limit of $25,000 for national party giving). Large donors and PACs would face tighter limits; leadership PACs would be phased out. Broadcasters and cable systems would be required to sell candidate advertising at half their lowest rate, keep the slots un-preempted, and risk license consequences for denying access. Incumbent members would lose election-year free mass mailings and the ability to spend campaign funds on personal expenses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, PACs, party committees, broadcasters

drawbacks.text: The spending limits are voluntary, so a wealthy self-funder or big-money candidate who refuses the cap could outspend a complying candidate; the bill's answer — automatically raising the complying candidate's limits and allowing extra contributions in response — could push total spending in contested races well above the $600,000 baseline rather than reducing it.

The broadcast discounts are not funded: stations are forced to give up half-price advertising revenue during peak campaign weeks, a real cost shifted to broadcasters (and ultimately their other advertisers and viewers) rather than paid by the Treasury.

As a trade for the soft money ban, the bill raises the individual limit for contributions to national parties from $20,000 to $25,000, channeling more regulated money into party treasuries — a concession critics on both sides would flag.

Capping campaign spending and mandating broadcast rates raise serious First Amendment questions; the bill itself anticipates litigation and fast-tracks Supreme Court review of its constitutionality, meaning its core could have been struck down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core gains — shutting down the soft money pipeline, real-time disclosure of attack ads, and a spending cap that lets non-wealthy candidates compete — are substantial and would have come at the direct expense of parties, PACs, big donors, and broadcasters rather than of ordinary taxpayers. The design has real weaknesses: the escalator provisions could raise spending in the very races the bill targets, the ad discounts shift a genuine cost onto broadcasters, and the constitutional risk to mandatory spending limits was significant. On balance this was a serious, bipartisan attempt to reduce the influence of concentrated money in elections; its main flaw was that it never got far enough to be amended or tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees, then to two subcommittees, and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Shays introduced the bill on January 21, 1997 with a bipartisan group of six original co-sponsors including Marty Meehan, and it was referred the same day to the House Oversight, Commerce, and Government Reform and Oversight Committees.
It attracted 46 cosponsors — 28 Democrats and 18 Republicans — showing support across both parties.
In February 1997 it was referred to a Telecommunications subcommittee and a Government Management subcommittee, splitting the bill across jurisdictions.
No committee ever held a hearing, reported the bill, or scheduled a vote; the record shows no action after those subcommittee referrals, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people who fund and profit from the existing system — national party committees, their soft-money donors, PACs, and broadcasters — kept the status quo untouched, and incumbent members kept their fundraising and free-mailing advantages.

for.name: Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship throughout the Congress.

for.name: Marty Meehan
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the lead Democratic co-sponsor at introduction, anchoring the bipartisan partnership.

against.name: House Oversight Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Oversight
against.what_they_did: Held the bill's primary jurisdiction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the record shows no committee action after the February 1997 subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Speaker
against.what_they_did: Split the bill's referral across three committees, including two where only narrow provisions fell under jurisdiction, and never scheduled it for a floor vote at any point in the two-year Congress.

against.name: Commerce and Government Reform Committee chairs
against.role: Chairs, House Commerce and House Government Reform and Oversight Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral — no hearings, no markups, no report — leaving it stranded with no path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was genuinely bipartisan — 28 Democrats and 18 Republicans cosponsored it — but the committees and leadership that declined to move it were all in the Republican majority, so the bill's death tracks party control even though its sponsorship did not.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: Soft money was the parties' principal funding channel; the bill would cut national committees off from it entirely and force state party federal-election spending into regulated funds. A raised $25,000 individual limit to national parties partly offsets the loss.

Stations would have to sell candidate ads at half their lowest rate during the final campaign weeks, keep the slots un-preempted, and face license conditions and revocation for denying access — a direct revenue and control cost, with a First Amendment takings dispute anticipated in the bill itself.

industries.industry: Political action committees and leadership PACs
industries.note: PAC money to House candidates would be capped at 25% of the spending limit, and leadership PACs — the vehicles members used to bankroll allies — would be abolished with forced disbursement of existing funds.
A new aggregate cap would limit large individual contributions to any House candidate, and the bill's spending-cap structure deliberately reduces the value of big checks to campaigns.
Contributions arranged or bundled through registered lobbyists would count against the lobbyist's own limits, closing a favored access-building channel.

Members would lose election-year franked mass mailings, personal use of campaign funds, and their soft-money solicitation privilege; they would keep their seats, and the voluntary spending cap would mostly bind challengers and open seats less than it binds well-financed incumbents.
